summary: The lecture defines GDP as the market value of final goods and services produced within a country's domestic territory during a specific period. It explains key concepts: monetary valuation, exclusion of illegal production, final vs intermediate goods to avoid double counting, and territorial scope including enclaves and domestic-operated assets abroad. GDP is a flow variable measured via three methods: value added, income, and expenditure, based on circular flow among households, firms, government, and external sector.
points: GDP = market value of final goods/services produced within domestic territory in a given period
GDP is a monetary concept; expressed in money terms, not physical quantities
Only legal market production included; illegal/contraband production excluded
Final goods exit production cycle; intermediate goods remain as inputs for further resale
Double counting avoided by counting only final goods; intermediate value embedded in them
All services are final (consumed at production, cannot be stored)
GDP is territorial: production within domestic territory counts regardless of producer nationality
Domestic territory includes political boundaries, territorial enclaves (embassies, bases abroad), domestic-operated aircraft/ships/rigs in international areas
GDP measures flow (production/income) in a period; excludes past production & secondhand goods; not wealth (stock)
Three GDP calculation methods: Value Added/Output/Production, Income, Expenditure

check.q: Which of the following is included in India's GDP according to the territorial concept?
opts: Cars produced by Honda in India
Services by TCS in Texas, USA
Secondhand car sales in current year

check.q: Why are intermediate goods excluded from GDP calculation?
opts: Their value is already embedded in final goods

check.q: Which of the following is NOT part of domestic territory for GDP calculation?
opts: Oil rig operated by Reliance in Venezuelan waters with exclusive rights
Indigo flight connecting Thailand and Portugal
